overview: Technology and Security covers what a risk practitioner must understand about technology to judge IT risk: architecture and roadmaps, operations, system development, data, projects, resilience and emerging technology, then security principles, awareness and privacy. The lens stays the same throughout: the practitioner analyzes the risk of each technology choice and advises, while business owners decide. AI runs through the domain, from model changes and training data to shadow AI and personal data in AI services.
analogy: Think of a busy airport. A master plan decides where new terminals go, so no one builds a runway on a whim. Ground crews log every change to an aircraft and dig into repeated faults, not just the latest delay. Unclaimed baggage is held for a set time and then disposed of properly. A backup control tower stands far enough away that one storm cannot close both. New ideas, like face-scan boarding, are piloted after weighing value against privacy. Security has many layers, and every worker can report something odd without fear of blame.

topics.overview: This topic covers how technology plans connect to business strategy: the enterprise architecture that shows how processes, data and systems fit together, the roadmap that schedules change, and the technical debt and legacy systems that build up risk when plans slip. The risk practitioner uses all three to see the business effect of a technology decision before it is made.
can_do: Explain how enterprise architecture helps judge the risk of a proposed system
Respond to technology bought outside the roadmap without banning it by reflex
Record legacy and technical-debt risk with a business owner and options

subtopics.name: Enterprise Architecture and Architecture Review
subtopics.definition: Enterprise architecture (EA) is the documented model of how business processes, data, applications and technology fit together to deliver the organization's strategy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: EA shows where a new system, vendor or AI service touches critical data and processes, so risk can be judged before money is committed. Without it, risk decisions are made one project at a time.
how_it_works: EA describes layers: business processes, data, applications and technology, and the links between them.
An architecture review board checks proposed solutions against approved principles, standards and the target architecture before funding.
Security and privacy requirements are built into the architecture, so each new system inherits them instead of reinventing them.
AI services are architecture components too: their data flows, model hosting and integrations belong in the EA.
Deviations from the architecture are recorded as exceptions with an owner, a reason and an expiry date.
subtopics.example: A regional utility plans to connect a vendor's AI chatbot directly to its customer billing database. Mateo, the IT risk analyst, compares the design with the enterprise architecture and finds the chatbot would bypass the approved integration layer that logs and filters customer data. Mateo documents the deviation and its risk, and takes it to the architecture review board with options.

review: Compare recent projects with the target architecture and approved standards
Sample open exceptions and confirm none has passed its expiry
evidence: Architecture review board minutes showing decisions and conditions
Exception register entries with owners and expiry dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the architecture review board record every deviation as a time-limited exception with a named business owner.
audit_focus.decides: The review board approves designs; the business owner accepts deviation risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: On CRISC items, EA is a risk tool, not a drawing. The practitioner uses it to see how a proposed change affects business processes and data, and brings deviations to the review board and the business owner rather than approving or blocking them alone.

exam_traps.trap: Treating enterprise architecture as an IT documentation exercise with no link to risk decisions.
exam_traps.why: EA earns its value when it shows the business impact of a change. A diagram nobody consults before approving projects reduces no risk.

key_terms.definition: A cross-functional group that checks proposed solutions against architecture principles and standards before approval.
The future state the organization plans to reach, used to judge whether new investments move toward it.
An approved, recorded deviation from an architecture standard, with an owner and an end date.

subtopics.memory_aid: EA answers one question first: what else does this change touch?

subtopics.name: Technology Roadmaps and Off-Roadmap Technology
subtopics.definition: A technology roadmap is a time-based plan showing which technologies the organization will adopt, upgrade or retire, and how each supports business goals.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A roadmap lets risk be planned: end-of-support dates, skills and funding are known years ahead. Technology bought outside it often arrives with no risk review, no support model and no owner.
how_it_works: The roadmap links each technology change to a business objective and a target date.
It flags known risk events in advance, such as vendor end of support or contract renewals.
Business-led purchases outside the roadmap still need a risk assessment and a named owner.
Each roadmap milestone should carry a risk assessment, not just a budget line.
Slippage is itself a risk signal when it delays the retirement of weak technology.
subtopics.example: Ayo, a risk analyst at a logistics firm, sees that the sales team has signed up for a route-planning software service with a corporate card. It is not on the technology roadmap and it holds customer addresses. Ayo asks the sales director, as business owner, to sponsor a risk assessment and logs the tool in the risk register while the assessment runs.

review: Compare purchasing and expense records with the approved technology roadmap
Sample upcoming milestones and look for missing risk assessments
evidence: Card and invoice data showing unapproved software subscriptions
Roadmap entries with end-of-support dates and linked risks
audit_focus.recommend: Have the IT steering committee require a risk assessment and named owner before any off-roadmap tool goes live.
audit_focus.decides: The accountable business manager makes the final call on the tool

subtopics.isaca_rule: Technology outside the roadmap is not banned by default; it is assessed. The practitioner makes the risk visible, finds the business owner and has the risk analyzed against appetite before anyone decides to keep, change or replace the tool.

exam_traps.trap: Blocking every purchase that is not on the roadmap.
exam_traps.why: A blanket ban pushes demand underground and may forgo real business value. The CRISC response is to assess the risk and let the owner decide within appetite.

key_terms.definition: Technology that staff or business units buy or use for work outside the enterprise's approval, security review and inventory.
The date after which a vendor stops providing patches, fixes or help for a product.

subtopics.name: Technical Debt and Legacy Systems
subtopics.definition: Technical debt is the future cost and risk created by shortcuts or aging technology, such as legacy systems that are hard to patch, change or support.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Legacy systems often run critical processes, so their weaknesses are business risks. Because they still work, the risk is easy to overlook until a failure, breach or skills gap makes it urgent.
how_it_works: Debt builds from deferred upgrades, quick fixes, custom code and unsupported components.
Risk grows over time: fewer patches, fewer people who understand the system and harder integrations.
Each legacy system needs a risk entry naming its business process, owner, weaknesses and compensating controls.
Options include upgrade, replace, isolate with compensating controls, or accept for a defined period.
A dated retirement plan turns open-ended debt into managed risk; until it is done, the register keeps the current rating, not the planned one.
subtopics.example: A hospital's pharmacy system runs on an operating system that lost vendor support two years ago. Staff say it is reliable, so no one has raised it. Nour, the IT risk analyst, records the risk with the pharmacy director proposed as owner, rates it against the hospital's appetite and sets out options: segment the system, buy extended support or fund replacement.

review: Compare the system inventory with vendor end-of-support dates
Sample unsupported systems and look for a register entry
evidence: Vulnerability scans showing missing patches on legacy systems
Register entries with compensating controls and review dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have each legacy system's business owner approve a dated plan to upgrade, isolate or replace it.
audit_focus.decides: The business owner signs any time-limited acceptance of legacy risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: 'It still works' is not a risk assessment. The practitioner registers legacy and technical-debt risk with a business owner, analyzes it against appetite and presents options; the owner chooses and may accept residual risk within appetite for a defined period, escalating anything beyond appetite to the level that set it.

exam_traps.trap: Leaving a legacy system off the risk register because it has run without failure for years.
exam_traps.why: Past reliability says little about exposure. Missing patches and shrinking skills raise likelihood over time, and the impact stays as high as the process it supports.

key_terms.definition: An older system still in use that is hard to support, change or secure with current methods.
An alternative control that reduces risk when a required control is missing, weak or cannot be applied.
A paid vendor arrangement that continues patches for a product past its normal end of support.
ISACA Glossary phrase for current risk once a planned response is implemented; KaiSip calls it target risk and uses it to judge the plan.

topics.topic_name: Operations Management (e.g., change management, assets, DevOps, problems, incidents)
topics.overview: This topic covers how IT runs day to day without creating unmanaged risk: controlled change and accurate configuration records, incident handling that restores service and problem management that removes causes, and DevOps pipelines where controls must be automated. The practitioner looks for whether impact was assessed, who approved, and whether the root cause is gone.
can_do: Tell a standard, normal and emergency change apart and say what each needs
Distinguish incident management from problem management in a scenario
Spot missing separation of duties in a CI/CD pipeline

subtopics.name: Change and Configuration Management
subtopics.definition: Change management is the controlled process for requesting, assessing, approving, testing, implementing and reviewing changes, with configuration management keeping an accurate record of approved settings.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many outages and security incidents follow a change. Controlled change keeps risk within appetite by making sure someone judged the impact, can undo the change and knows what the system should look like.
how_it_works: Each change has a request, an impact assessment, an approval suited to its risk, a test result and a back-out plan.
Emergency changes may bypass the normal approval path, usually through an emergency approver, but are documented and reviewed after the fact as soon as practical.

A configuration management database (CMDB) records configuration items and dependencies; assets missing from it sit outside patching, change and backup, so differing counts from other tools are reconciled.
Comparing live settings with the baseline finds unauthorized changes, which are investigated, not quietly reversed.
Low-risk, repeatable changes can be pre-approved, so review effort follows risk.
A growing share of emergency changes is analyzed for its cause, such as slow normal approvals or poor planning, before more approval steps are added.

types.meaning: Pre-approved, low-risk and repeatable, carried out from a set procedure.
Assessed and approved by the change authority before it is made.
Made fast to restore service or stop harm through an expedited approval, then documented and reviewed after the fact.

subtopics.example: At a city council, Ines, a risk analyst, reviews the month's changes and finds that a third were marked emergency, including routine firewall updates. Several have no after-the-fact review. Ines reports the pattern to the head of IT operations, with the risk that the emergency route is being used to avoid assessment.

review: Sample emergency tickets and measure days until after-the-fact sign-off
Compare live configurations with approved baselines for unexplained drift
evidence: Change tickets with approver names, test evidence and rollback steps
Configuration drift reports from monitoring tools
audit_focus.recommend: Have the change manager analyze why emergency changes are rising, then set emergency-change criteria and report volume and overdue reviews monthly.
audit_focus.decides: The change authority approves changes; the risk owner accepts any remaining change risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: The risk view of change asks: was the impact assessed, approved by the right authority and reversible? Emergency changes are allowed, but each gets a timely retrospective review. Growing emergency volume is a risk signal: report it and find out why the normal path is being avoided.

exam_traps.trap: Accepting an emergency change as complete once service is restored.
exam_traps.why: Skipping approval is allowed only because a review follows. Without it, untested or unauthorized changes stay in production and the control quietly fails.

key_terms.definition: The tested steps to undo a change and restore the previous state if it fails.
The approved, documented set of settings for a system, used to detect drift.
A group that assesses and advises on higher-risk changes before the change authority approves them.

subtopics.name: Incident and Problem Management
subtopics.definition: Incident management restores normal service quickly after a disruption; problem management finds and removes the root cause so the incident does not happen again.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fixing symptoms without the cause lets the same failure recur, often at a worse time. Repeat incidents raise likelihood, and an unknown root cause hides what really needs a control.
how_it_works: An incident is recorded, classified by business impact, prioritized, resolved and closed.
A problem is opened when incidents repeat, a major incident occurs or a trend appears.
Root cause analysis finds why it happened; a known error records the cause and any workaround.
A permanent fix usually goes through change management, so problem and change processes connect.
Incident and problem trends feed the risk register and key risk indicators.
When a permanent fix is costly or unfunded, the risk and options go to the owner of the affected business process; IT does not accept it by default.

rows.label: Trigger
cells: Repeat incidents, a major incident or a trend

rows.label: Typical output
cells: Known error, workaround, permanent fix through change

subtopics.example: A university's student portal crashes five times in one semester, each time fixed by restarting a server. Every ticket is closed within an hour, so the service desk reports good performance. Kofi, the IT risk analyst, sees the pattern, asks for a problem record and links the recurring outage to the enrollment-period risk scenario in the register.

review: Analyze incident records for repeats with the same symptom or cause
Trace major incidents to a problem record and root cause
evidence: Incident trend reports grouped by service and cause
Problem tickets naming the confirmed cause and the fixing change
audit_focus.recommend: Have the problem manager open problem records for repeat incidents and report open root causes to service owners.
audit_focus.decides: The service owner prioritizes permanent fixes; the risk owner accepts recurrence risk meanwhile

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fast incident closure is not risk reduction. The practitioner looks for repeats and asks for problem management to find the root cause, then checks that the fix goes through change control and that the risk entry reflects the new likelihood.

exam_traps.trap: Judging the process healthy because incidents are closed quickly.
exam_traps.why: Quick closure measures the service desk's speed. Repeated incidents with the same cause mean the risk is unchanged and likely to recur.

key_terms.definition: A structured method for finding the underlying reason an event happened, not just its visible symptom.
A problem whose root cause is identified and documented, often with a workaround.
A temporary way to reduce or avoid an incident's impact until a permanent fix is in place.

subtopics.name: DevOps and Pipeline Controls
subtopics.definition: DevOps joins development and operations so software moves to production through an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Pipelines can push changes many times a day, so manual approvals cannot keep up. If controls are not built into the pipeline, one person or one stolen account can put unreviewed code straight into production.
how_it_works: Controls move into the pipeline: automated tests, security scans and policy checks gate each release.
Separation of duties is kept by requiring a second person to review and approve code before merge.
Pipeline accounts, secrets and build tools are protected, because whoever controls the pipeline controls production.
Infrastructure as code puts server and network settings under the same review and version control as software.
Pipeline logs record every change, which supports both monitoring and audit.
subtopics.example: Hana, a risk analyst at a payments start-up, learns that any of the five engineers can merge their own code and deploy it, and the pipeline's deployment key is shared in a chat channel. Hana maps the risk to the fraud-loss scenario in the register and works with the engineering lead, as control owner, on peer review and secret storage options.

review: Inspect pipeline settings for self-approval or bypass of required reviews
Trace production deployments to an approved, reviewed code change
evidence: Branch-protection and approval settings exported from the repository
Pipeline logs linking each deployment to its reviewer
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engineering lead enforce independent review before merge and move pipeline secrets into a managed vault.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts residual pipeline risk; the engineering lead is accountable for its controls

subtopics.isaca_rule: Speed does not remove the need for separation of duties; it moves the control into the pipeline. The practitioner checks that no single person can write, approve and deploy a change, and that the pipeline itself is protected as a critical asset.

exam_traps.trap: Assuming automated testing alone makes DevOps safe.
exam_traps.why: Tests check only what they were written to check. Without independent review and protected pipeline access, one person can still push harmful or unauthorized code.

key_terms.definition: Managing servers and networks through version-controlled configuration files instead of manual setup.
A credential, such as a deployment key or token, that the pipeline uses to act on production systems.
A second developer checks and approves code before it is merged.

topics.overview: This topic covers risk at each phase of building or buying a system: early security and privacy requirements, secure development and testing, acceptance by business users, and review after go-live. It also treats AI models as systems with their own life cycle, where retraining and new versions are changes that need validation and approval.
can_do: Name the risk activity that belongs in each SDLC phase
Explain why security requirements belong in design, not at go-live
Apply change control to a retrained or replaced AI model

subtopics.name: Risk Across the SDLC Phases
subtopics.definition: The system development life cycle (SDLC) is the sequence of phases from initiation through design, build, testing, implementation, operation and disposal, each with its own risk activities.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A flaw found in design costs little to fix; the same flaw found after go-live costs far more and may already have caused harm. Risk activities in every phase keep the project within appetite.
how_it_works: Initiation: confirm the business case, owner, data sensitivity and an initial risk assessment, and update that assessment whenever the scope or data changes.
Requirements and design: define security, privacy and control requirements alongside functional ones; for a purchased system, put them in the selection criteria and contract.
Build and test: verify requirements are met; business users, not developers, sign off acceptance testing.
Implementation: confirm the owner accepts residual risk within appetite, or orders more treatment, before go-live.
Post-implementation review: check whether benefits arrived and risks stayed within appetite.
Disposal: retire data and components securely.
subtopics.example: A retailer is rebuilding its loyalty app, and the project plan schedules the only security review two weeks before launch. Teo, the risk analyst, shows the sponsor that a late finding could force a costly redesign or a launch with open risk, and proposes adding security and privacy requirements to the design phase gate.

review: Trace each project phase gate to a completed risk assessment
Inspect acceptance sign-offs for developer names instead of business users
evidence: Phase gate records showing risk and control sign-offs
Signed acceptance test results and go-live risk acceptance
audit_focus.recommend: Have the project sponsor make risk and security sign-off a condition of every phase gate.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner, the business manager accountable for the system, signs the go-live risk acceptance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Risk is assessed at every SDLC phase, starting at initiation. The best time to set a control requirement is the earliest phase, and before launch the risk owner accepts residual risk within appetite or requires more treatment; developers and the practitioner never accept it.

exam_traps.trap: Treating a small change as too minor to need a risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Small code changes can touch critical data or controls. The depth of assessment can scale with risk, but every change gets one.

exam_traps.trap: Letting developers perform user acceptance testing.
exam_traps.why: Developers test what they built against their own understanding. Business users confirm the system meets their needs, which keeps the check independent.

key_terms.definition: A decision point where a project must meet set criteria before moving to the next phase.
Testing by business users to confirm a system meets their requirements before go-live.
A review after go-live of whether the project delivered its benefits and kept risk within appetite.

subtopics.name: Secure Development and Testing
subtopics.definition: Secure development builds security into how software is designed, coded, tested and maintained, following a framework such as the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most exploitable flaws start as design or coding mistakes. A secure process lowers the number of vulnerabilities released and shows owners, customers and regulators that software risk is managed.
how_it_works: The SSDF groups practices into four areas: prepare the organization, protect the software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities.
Security requirements are defined early and checked through threat modeling, code review and testing.
Testing combines static analysis, dynamic testing and, for high-risk systems, penetration testing.
Third-party and open-source components are tracked and checked for known vulnerabilities.
When a vulnerability is found, its root cause is analyzed so the process improves, not just the code.
subtopics.example: A health insurer's developers keep fixing the same input-validation flaw in different apps after each penetration test. Wei, the IT risk analyst, notes the repeat findings in the risk register and asks the head of development, as control owner, to treat the cause: secure coding standards, training and an automated check in the build.

review: Compare repeat test findings across releases to spot unfixed root causes
Trace security requirements from design into test cases
evidence: Static and dynamic scan results with remediation dates
Secure coding standard and developer training records
audit_focus.recommend: Have the development manager add automated security checks to the build and track repeat findings to root cause.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts residual software risk at release

subtopics.isaca_rule: Testing finds flaws; a secure development process prevents them. The practitioner looks for root causes behind repeat findings and favors controls built into the process over late testing; the control owner is accountable for choosing those controls and keeping them working.

exam_traps.trap: Relying on a penetration test just before release as the main security control.
exam_traps.why: A late test finds some flaws when they are costliest to fix and leaves the process that created them unchanged.

key_terms.definition: Automated review of source code for weaknesses without running the program.
Testing a running application to find weaknesses an attacker could exploit.
A list of the components and libraries inside a piece of software, used to track known vulnerabilities.

subtopics.name: AI Models in the SDLC
subtopics.definition: AI models follow a life cycle of design, data preparation, training, validation, deployment, monitoring and retraining, and each new model version is a change to control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A retrained model can behave differently even when no code changed. Without version control, validation and approval, a model update can quietly add bias, errors or new exposure to business decisions.
how_it_works: Each model version is recorded with its training data, settings, test results and approver.
Retraining or replacing a model goes through change management, with validation against agreed performance and fairness criteria.
The model's business owner approves deployment; data scientists build and test it.
Production monitoring watches for drift, the gradual loss of accuracy as real-world data changes.
A rollback plan lets the team return to the previous version if the new one misbehaves.
Edits to an AI system's instructions, prompts or settings change its behavior too, so they are tested and approved like code before reaching users.
subtopics.example: An insurer's claims team retrains its fraud-scoring model every month with new data, and data scientists push each version live themselves. Elif, the risk analyst, finds that one release doubled false fraud flags for a single region. Elif records the risk and proposes a release gate: validation results reviewed and approved by the claims director before deployment.

review: Trace production model versions to validation results and approval
Compare monitored model performance with agreed thresholds
evidence: Model registry entries with data version, tests and approver
Accuracy and false-alert trend reports for live models
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner require validation sign-off and a rollback plan before any retrained model is deployed.
audit_focus.decides: The accountable business owner signs off each model release

subtopics.isaca_rule: A model change is a change. Retraining, new data or a new model version needs validation, approval by the business owner and a rollback plan, the same as code. The practitioner checks that the gate exists; owners decide what risk is acceptable.

exam_traps.trap: Treating retraining as routine maintenance that needs no change approval.
exam_traps.why: New training data can change model behavior as much as new code. Without validation and approval, errors and bias reach production unseen.

key_terms.definition: Loss of model accuracy over time because real-world data no longer matches the training data.
Testing, ideally independent, that a model meets agreed accuracy, fairness and robustness criteria before use.
A controlled record of model versions, their training data, test results and approvals.

topics.overview: This topic follows data from creation to destruction: who owns it, how classification sets its handling, how long it is kept and how it is made unrecoverable at the end. It also applies the same life cycle to AI training data, where source, quality and lawful use decide whether a model can be trusted.
can_do: Tell the data owner's decisions from the custodian's duties
Explain why deleting is not sanitizing and choose clear, purge or destroy
Challenge a keep-everything retention habit with the risk it creates
Check the source and fitness of data before it trains a model

subtopics.name: Data Lifecycle, Classification and Ownership
subtopics.definition: Data lifecycle management controls data through each stage, create, store, use, share, archive and destroy, according to its classification and its owner's rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Data risk changes at each stage: sharing brings new parties, archives get forgotten and old copies outlive their purpose. Classification and a named owner make protection match value and sensitivity.
how_it_works: The data owner, a business manager, classifies data and decides who may access it and for how long.
The data custodian, often IT, applies the owner's rules through storage, backup and access controls.
Classification levels set handling rules, such as encryption, sharing limits and retention.
A data inventory shows where each class of data lives, including copies in test and analytics systems.
Each stage has controls: input checks at creation, access control in use, agreements when shared.
Data that no business unit claims is reported so senior management can assign an owner; IT protects it as custodian in the meantime.

rows.label: Typical role
cells: Business manager accountable for the data
IT or a service provider running the systems

rows.label: Decides
cells: How to carry out the owner's rules

subtopics.example: A university research office finds that a database of participant health surveys has been copied into three analytics workspaces, and nobody can say who approved the copies. Bruno, the risk analyst, traces the dataset to the research director as data owner and asks them to confirm its classification and decide which copies are justified.

review: Trace sensitive datasets in the inventory to a named business owner
Compare copies in test and analytics systems with approved uses
evidence: Data inventory or catalog showing classification and owner
Access reviews signed by data owners
audit_focus.recommend: Have each data owner confirm classification and approve every copy of sensitive data outside its home system.
audit_focus.decides: The accountable business manager decides who may use the data

subtopics.isaca_rule: Data belongs to the business, not to IT. The practitioner finds the data owner and makes sure classification, access and retention decisions are theirs; IT, as custodian, carries them out. Data with no owner is a risk to report.

exam_traps.trap: Naming IT as the data owner because IT runs the systems that store it.
exam_traps.why: IT holds and protects the data but cannot judge its business value or who should use it. Ownership sits with the accountable business manager.

key_terms.definition: Grouping data by sensitivity and value so each group gets matching handling rules.
A record of what data the organization holds, where, in what form and under whose ownership.

subtopics.name: Retention and Sanitization
subtopics.definition: Retention sets how long each type of data is kept, and sanitization makes data on storage media unrecoverable once it is no longer needed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Data kept past its purpose adds breach impact, legal exposure and cost with no business value. Data removed the wrong way may still be recoverable when equipment is reused, sold or discarded.
how_it_works: A retention schedule sets periods by data type, based on legal, regulatory and business needs.
At the end of the period, data is disposed of unless a legal hold requires it to be kept.
Deleting a file usually removes only the pointer to it; the data can often still be recovered.
NIST SP 800-88 describes three sanitization methods, chosen by data sensitivity and media type.
Sanitization is verified and recorded, including when a vendor handles disposal.

types.meaning: Overwrites or resets data through normal interfaces; protects against simple recovery tools.
Uses methods such as cryptographic erase, which works only if the data was encrypted from the start, to defeat laboratory-level recovery.
Shreds, melts or pulverizes media so recovery is infeasible and the media cannot be reused.

subtopics.example: A dental practice group keeps every patient record since 1998 on a file server because no one wants to delete anything. Lena, the risk consultant, shows the practice director that the oldest records are past their legal retention periods but would still count in a breach, and proposes a retention schedule with verified disposal.

review: Compare stored data ages with the approved retention schedule
Sample disposed devices and trace each to a sanitization record
evidence: Storage reports showing data older than retention periods
Sanitization certificates from internal teams or disposal vendors
audit_focus.recommend: Have data owners approve a retention schedule with legal counsel and require verified sanitization of all retired media.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner signs off retention periods after legal review

subtopics.isaca_rule: Keep data while a legal or business need exists, then dispose of it in a verified way: scheduled, logged deletion for live records and sanitization for media leaving use. Keeping everything just in case raises risk. The data owner sets retention with legal advice.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping all data indefinitely in case it is needed later.
exam_traps.why: Every extra record adds breach impact and legal discovery exposure. Retention should end when the legal or business need ends.

exam_traps.trap: Treating file deletion or a quick reformat as secure disposal of media being reused, sold or discarded.
exam_traps.why: Deletion often leaves data recoverable. Sanitization must match the media and data sensitivity, and be verified.

key_terms.definition: A list setting how long each type of record is kept and when it is disposed of.
A requirement to preserve data relevant to litigation or an investigation, overriding normal disposal.
A record showing which media were sanitized, by what method, when and by whom.

subtopics.name: AI Training Data Through the Lifecycle
subtopics.definition: AI training data management applies the data lifecycle to data used to train, test and tune models, from sourcing and labeling through retention and deletion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A model reflects its data. Poor, biased, poisoned or unlawfully sourced training data becomes poor or unlawful decisions, and personal data inside a model can be hard to remove later.
how_it_works: Sourcing: record where data came from, the right to use it and whether it contains personal data.
Preparation: check quality, labeling accuracy and coverage of real cases before training.
Protection: restrict access to training sets and watch for tampering, which can poison the model.
Lineage: link each model version to the exact data version used to train it.
Retention and deletion: apply the retention schedule to training sets and plan how deletion requests affect trained models.
subtopics.example: A recruitment platform wants to train a candidate-matching model on ten years of past hiring decisions. Ravi, the risk analyst, points out that the history may encode past bias and holds personal data collected for a different purpose. Ravi asks the product owner to sponsor a data review and a privacy assessment before training starts.

review: Trace training datasets to their source, usage rights and owner
Compare training data coverage with the populations the model serves
evidence: Dataset documentation with source, consent basis and quality checks
Lineage records linking model versions to data versions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the model owner require documented data sourcing, quality and privacy review before any training run.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner permits training use; the use case's risk owner accepts model risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Training data is data: it needs an owner, a lawful source, quality checks and a retention period. The practitioner asks where the data came from and whether it fits the purpose before the model is built, not after it misbehaves.

exam_traps.trap: Assuming any data the organization already holds can be used to train a model.
exam_traps.why: Data collected for one purpose may not be lawful or fair to reuse for training, and its quality or bias may be unknown.

key_terms.definition: A traceable record of where data came from and how it was changed before use.
Deliberately tampering with training data so a model learns harmful or wrong behavior.
Training data that reflects the range of real cases the model will face in use.

topics.overview: This topic covers how the organization chooses and delivers technology investments: a portfolio ranked by value and risk together, and projects, including Agile ones, that track risk in their backlog and definition of done. The practitioner makes sure project risks that will outlive the project reach the enterprise register and the right owner.
can_do: Rank investments on value and risk, not cost or sponsor influence alone
Show where risk lives in an Agile backlog and definition of done
Escalate a deferred control to the business owner before release

subtopics.name: Portfolio Management by Value and Risk
subtopics.definition: Portfolio management selects, prioritizes and balances the organization's programs and projects by their expected value, risk and fit with strategy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Money and people are limited. A portfolio view stops low-value, high-risk projects from consuming resources and shows senior management the combined risk of everything in flight.
how_it_works: Each proposal states its business value, cost, risks and link to strategic objectives.
Proposals are scored on value and risk together, not on cost or sponsor influence alone.
The portfolio is reviewed regularly; projects whose value falls or risk rises are changed, paused or stopped.
Projects can also reduce risk, such as retiring a weak system, and that benefit counts in scoring.
Dependencies between projects are tracked, since one delay can push risk into others.
subtopics.example: A city transit authority's steering group ranks nine technology proposals by cost alone. Amara, the enterprise risk analyst, adds a risk column and shows that a mid-ranked upgrade would remove a weakness behind fare collection, a top-rated scenario, while the cheapest proposal adds a new vendor dependency. Amara presents both views to the steering group.

review: Compare funded projects with their value and risk scores
Trace stopped or paused projects to documented portfolio decisions
evidence: Portfolio scoring sheets showing value, risk and strategic fit
Committee minutes recording funding choices and stated reasons
audit_focus.recommend: Have the investment committee score every proposal on value and risk together and review the portfolio quarterly.
audit_focus.decides: The investment committee approves, prioritizes and stops investments

subtopics.isaca_rule: Portfolio decisions balance value and risk against strategy. The practitioner supplies the risk view, including the risks a project would reduce, so senior management can prioritize; the investment committee decides.

exam_traps.trap: Ranking projects by cost or return alone and leaving risk to each project team.
exam_traps.why: Two projects with equal return can carry very different risk. Without a risk view the portfolio may concentrate exposure the enterprise cannot tolerate.

key_terms.definition: A group of related projects managed together to deliver a shared business outcome.
The senior management body that approves, prioritizes and stops technology investments.
Tracking whether a completed investment delivers the value promised in its business case.

subtopics.name: Project Risk and Agile Delivery
subtopics.definition: Project risk is uncertainty that can affect a project's scope, time, cost or quality; in Agile delivery it is managed in short, repeated cycles.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Project risks often become operational IT risks after go-live. If they are tracked only inside the project, or dropped to meet a date, the enterprise inherits exposure no one approved.
how_it_works: Project risks are logged with owners and linked to the enterprise risk register when they could outlast the project.
In Agile, risk items and security tasks sit in the backlog and are prioritized alongside features.
The definition of done includes security, privacy and control criteria, so work is not finished without them.
Sprint reviews and retrospectives are natural points to update risk status.
Agile reduces heavy documents, not risk records: decisions and accepted risks are still recorded.
At project closure, open risks that continue into operation move to the enterprise register with an operational owner; they do not close with the project.
subtopics.example: A bank's mobile team works in two-week sprints and has postponed its fraud-control stories for four sprints to hit a launch date. Zara, the IT risk analyst, raises the deferred stories as a project risk that will become an operational fraud risk at launch, and asks the product owner to review it with the business sponsor.

review: Trace deferred security and control stories to a recorded risk decision
Inspect sample stories closed as done for missing control criteria
evidence: Backlog history showing deferred risk items and their age
Enterprise register entries that originated in project logs
audit_focus.recommend: Have the product owner record every deferred control as a risk and escalate it to the business owner before release.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts project risk that reaches operations

subtopics.isaca_rule: Agile changes how risk is handled, not whether. The practitioner looks for risk in the backlog, definition of done and register, and escalates deferred controls to the risk owner, the business manager whose process the system will serve; dropping risk work to meet a date is that owner's informed decision.

exam_traps.trap: Believing Agile projects do not need documented risk decisions.
exam_traps.why: Agile favors working software over heavy paperwork, but accepted risks and control decisions still need a record and an accountable owner.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping the project risk log separate from the enterprise risk register.
exam_traps.why: Risks that outlive the project, such as a weak control at launch, must reach the enterprise view so the right owner can accept or treat them.

key_terms.definition: The prioritized list of work items, including features, fixes and risk tasks, for an Agile team.
The agreed criteria every work item must meet before it counts as complete.
The person accountable for the backlog's priorities and the value the team delivers.

topics.overview: This topic covers how technology keeps critical processes running through disruption: recovery strategies and alternate sites built to meet recovery objectives, backups that survive ransomware and can actually be restored, and tests that prove the plan works. The practitioner judges each against business tolerance for downtime and data loss.
can_do: Match hot, warm, cold and cloud recovery to RTO, RPO and cost
Find a single point of failure shared by primary and recovery sites
Put ransomware recovery steps in the right order
Choose a recovery test type that fits plan maturity and risk

subtopics.name: Recovery Strategies and Alternate Sites
subtopics.definition: Recovery strategies are planned ways to restore systems after a disruption, such as hot, warm or cold sites or cloud failover, chosen to meet recovery objectives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The strategy decides whether the business recovers within its tolerance for downtime and data loss. Too little capability breaches tolerance; too much wastes money.
how_it_works: Through the business impact analysis, process owners set each critical process's MTO, an RTO within it, and an RPO from the data loss they can tolerate.
The strategy must meet RTO and RPO by design, at a cost the owner accepts.
An alternate site is placed so the same event cannot disable both sites.
Shared dependencies, such as one network carrier, identity service or power feed, are single points of failure.
Cloud recovery is a shared responsibility: the contract sets who restores what, often the platform but not data the customer's users delete; the customer stays accountable for its data.

rows.label: Ready state
cells: Equipped and configured, with current or near-current data
Some hardware and connectivity; data restored on arrival

subtopics.example: A food distributor's recovery site is across the street from its data center, on the same substation and flood plain. Dara, the risk analyst, maps both sites to the flood scenario and shows the operations director that one flood would take out both, breaching order processing's four-hour RTO.

review: Walk through the recovery timeline for one critical process against its RTO and RPO
Trace shared dependencies between primary and alternate sites
evidence: Approved impact analysis listing recovery targets by process
Recovery test results showing actual restore times
audit_focus.recommend: Have the business continuity manager remove shared dependencies or present the residual gap to process owners.
audit_focus.decides: The process owner signs off the chosen strategy and its cost

subtopics.isaca_rule: A recovery strategy is judged by whether it meets the RTO and RPO under the scenarios that matter. The practitioner finds shared single points of failure and reports the gap; the business owner chooses the strategy and accepts its cost and residual risk within appetite.

exam_traps.trap: Counting a recovery site as adequate because it exists and is equipped.
exam_traps.why: A site exposed to the same hazard, network or supplier as the primary fails with it; independence matters as much as equipment.

key_terms.definition: The target for how soon a business function, or a resource it depends on, must be working again after a disruption, set within the MTO.
How far back in time recovered data may be after a disruption, set by the data loss the business accepts; it drives backup frequency.
ISACA term for the outage limit of a critical process or system, past which damage becomes significant; recovery must finish within it. Others say MTD.
ISACA term: how long a system can stay down before the business can no longer meet its objectives.

subtopics.name: Backups and Ransomware Recovery
subtopics.definition: Backups are protected copies of data and systems kept so they can be restored after loss, corruption or attack, including ransomware.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Backups are often the last control against ransomware and destructive attacks. If attackers can reach or encrypt them, or restores fail, the organization faces long outages or pressure to pay.
how_it_works: A common rule of thumb keeps at least three copies, on two kinds of media, with one offsite or offline.
Immutable or offline copies cannot be changed or deleted by an attacker who gains administrator access.
Backup frequency is set by the RPO; restore speed must support the RTO.
In ransomware recovery, contain the attack first, then verify backups are clean before restoring.
Restores are tested regularly, because a backup that was never restored is an untested assumption.
A useful key control indicator for backups is the share of test restores that meet the RTO and RPO, not the share of backup jobs completed.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm's backups run nightly and the console shows green every day. Sam, the IT risk analyst, asks when a full restore was last tested; the answer is never. Sam records the risk that the RTO for the dispatch system is unproven and proposes a scheduled restore test to the infrastructure manager.

review: Inspect backup architecture for offline or immutable copies
Sample restore tests and compare actual times with the RTO
evidence: Restore test reports with dates, scope and restore times
Backup configuration showing retention, immutability and access rights
audit_focus.recommend: Have the infrastructure manager schedule regular restore tests and keep one immutable or offline copy of critical data.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts residual recovery risk based on test results

subtopics.isaca_rule: A backup counts only when it is protected from the threat and has been restored successfully. In ransomware recovery the order is contain, verify the backup is clean, then restore; the practitioner advises on that order and the risk of skipping it, while the incident lead and business owner decide.

exam_traps.trap: Restoring from backup immediately after ransomware is discovered.
exam_traps.why: If the attacker still has access, or the backup holds the malware, restored systems are encrypted again. Contain the attack and verify backup integrity first.

exam_traps.trap: Treating successful backup jobs as proof that recovery will work.
exam_traps.why: A job log shows data was copied, not that it can be restored within the RTO. Only a restore test proves that.

key_terms.definition: A backup copy that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, even by administrators.
Three copies of data, on two types of media, with one copy kept offsite or offline.
A trial recovery from backup to prove data or a system can be restored within the RTO.

subtopics.name: Testing Recovery Capability
subtopics.definition: Recovery testing checks that disaster recovery capability, and the technology side of continuity plans, works, using methods that range from checklist reviews and tabletop exercises to full interruption tests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An untested plan is an assumption. Tests show whether RTO and RPO are met, whether people know their roles and where the gaps are, so owners can decide on fixes before a real event.
how_it_works: Tests are chosen by risk and plan maturity, starting with low-disruption methods and building to realistic ones.
Each test has objectives tied to RTO, RPO and the scenarios in the risk register.
Observers record what worked, what failed and how long recovery actually took.
Findings go into a corrective action plan with owners and dates, and the plan is retested.

types.meaning: Plan owners confirm contacts, steps and resources are current.
Key people talk through a scenario to test roles, decisions and communication.
Teams carry out parts of the plan, such as restoring one system.
Systems are recovered at the alternate site while production keeps running.
Production is actually moved to recovery systems; the most realistic and most disruptive test.

subtopics.example: A city water utility runs its first tabletop exercise on a ransomware scenario. Within an hour the team finds that no one knows who may authorize switching treatment controls to manual operation. Aiko, the risk analyst, records the gap, links it to the ransomware scenario in the register and asks the operations director to assign the decision authority.

review: Compare tested scenarios with the top-rated scenarios in the register
Trace test findings to corrective actions and retest dates
evidence: Test reports with objectives, actual recovery times and gaps
Action tracker listing overdue items and responsible managers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the business continuity manager tie each test to a register scenario and track findings to closure.
audit_focus.decides: Process owners agree how much test disruption to tolerate

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recovery capability is proven by testing, not by having a plan. The practitioner checks that tests match the risk scenarios, that findings get owners and dates, and that results update the risk assessment; the business owner decides how much test disruption to accept.

exam_traps.trap: Starting with a full interruption test to get the most realistic result.
exam_traps.why: A full interruption test can itself cause an outage. Organizations build up from tabletop and functional tests and run full tests only when the plan is mature and the risk is accepted.

key_terms.definition: A list of fixes from a test or review, each with an owner and a due date.
The realistic event, such as a ransomware attack or flood, that a recovery test is built around.

topics.overview: This topic covers how the risk practitioner evaluates new technology such as cloud services, AI and machine learning, the Internet of Things, blockchain and quantum computing. The task is to weigh threats, vulnerabilities and opportunities against business objectives and appetite, then recommend conditions, so leaders neither ban by reflex nor adopt on vendor claims.
can_do: Weigh the opportunity of a new technology alongside its threats
Replace a reflex ban with a conditional, risk-assessed pilot
Make sure each AI use case has an owner, an inventory entry and oversight

subtopics.name: Evaluating Emerging Technologies
subtopics.definition: Evaluating emerging technology means assessing a new technology's threats, vulnerabilities and opportunities for the business before and during adoption.
subtopics.why_it_matters: New technology can create advantage, new exposure or both. The ISACA Glossary's enterprise risk management exploits risk as well as controlling it, to increase stakeholder value, so leaders weigh both instead of banning by reflex or adopting blind.
how_it_works: Start from the business objective the technology would serve and the value it could add.
Identify new threats and vulnerabilities, including those inherited from vendors and integrations.
Check vendor claims through evidence, pilots and independent assessments, not marketing material.
Compare the risk with appetite and propose conditions, such as a limited pilot, extra controls or exit terms.
Track the technology as an emerging risk and revisit the assessment as it matures.
With little data, record the risk early as an emerging risk with stated uncertainty, a proposed owner and a review date, rather than waiting for losses.

types.meaning: Fast scaling and new features; shared responsibility and dependence on a few providers.
Real-time data from devices; weak default security and devices that are hard to patch.
Tamper-evident shared records; key management risk and errors that are hard to reverse.
Future computing power that could break today's public-key encryption, so cryptography inventories and migration plans matter.

subtopics.example: A farm cooperative's operations head wants soil sensors linked to a cloud dashboard to cut fertilizer costs, while some board members want to block the idea over security fears. Luca, the risk analyst, assesses both the savings and the risks, such as default device passwords and vendor lock-in, and proposes a limited pilot with conditions for the board to consider.

review: Compare the technology's business case with its risk assessment
Trace vendor security claims to independent evidence or pilot results
evidence: Pilot results showing value achieved and issues found
Emerging risk entries with review dates and owners
audit_focus.recommend: Have the sponsoring executive approve adoption conditions, such as pilot scope and exit terms, before scaling.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides adoption within the approved risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Emerging technology is neither banned nor adopted on faith. The practitioner assesses threats, vulnerabilities and opportunities against the business objective and appetite, then recommends conditions; senior management decides whether to adopt.

exam_traps.trap: Recommending a ban on a new technology because its risks are not yet understood.
exam_traps.why: Uncertainty calls for assessment, not prohibition. A ban can forgo value and push staff toward unmanaged workarounds.

exam_traps.trap: Judging a new platform on vendor claims, certifications and features alone.
exam_traps.why: Claims and certifications describe the product, not its fit with the organization's data and appetite, or a way out if a young vendor fails. That needs evidence and exit terms.

key_terms.definition: A possible future event or condition that would help the enterprise meet its objectives if it happened.
Encryption methods designed to resist attack by future quantum computers, such as the NIST FIPS 203 standard.
Dependence on one supplier that makes switching costly or slow.

subtopics.name: AI and Machine Learning Adoption
subtopics.definition: AI adoption risk covers the threats and opportunities of using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in business processes, from vendor tools to in-house models.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI can speed decisions and cut costs, but errors, bias, data leakage and opaque behavior can harm customers and breach law at scale. The risk sits with the business process that relies on the AI.
how_it_works: Each AI use case has a business owner, a stated purpose and an entry in the AI inventory and risk register.
Assessment covers data, accuracy, bias, security threats such as prompt injection, privacy and legal duties.
Higher-impact uses need human oversight, such as review of AI decisions before they affect people.
Third-party AI is assessed like any supplier, with contract terms on data use and model changes.
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) structures the work in four functions: govern, map, measure and manage.
subtopics.example: A bank's contact center wants a generative AI assistant to draft replies to customers. Mina, the risk analyst, asks the contact center director, as process owner, to define what the assistant may answer, then assesses wrong-answer rates, prompt injection and what customer data the vendor keeps. Mina presents the findings with options for agent review before replies are sent.

review: Compare network and expense data on AI services with the inventory
Trace high-impact AI decisions to human review records
evidence: Inventory records with risk ratings and named accountable managers
Bias and accuracy results from pre-deployment testing
audit_focus.recommend: Have each AI use case owner complete a risk assessment and define human oversight before go-live.
audit_focus.decides: The business process owner accepts AI risk within appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI risk is business risk with a business owner. The practitioner makes sure each AI use is inventoried, assessed against appetite before go-live and monitored after; the owner decides, and higher-impact uses keep a human in the loop.

exam_traps.trap: Treating an AI tool as low risk because a reputable vendor supplies it.
exam_traps.why: The vendor's model may be sound, but the organization's use, data and decisions create the risk. The deploying organization stays accountable.

key_terms.definition: A record of AI systems in use, with owner, purpose, data and risk rating.
People able to review, override or stop AI outputs before they cause harm.
Crafted input that makes an AI system ignore its instructions or reveal data.

topics.overview: This topic covers the principles behind sound security, from confidentiality, integrity and availability to defense in depth, least privilege and separation of duties, plus Zero Trust and the frameworks used to organize and benchmark security. The practitioner uses them to judge whether a control set fits the risk, remembering that framework alignment or certification is evidence, not proof of low risk.
can_do: Spot a control set that depends on one layer or one person
Explain Zero Trust as a risk-reducing strategy rather than a product
Check a certificate's scope before relying on it
Use a framework profile to find and prioritize gaps

subtopics.name: Core Security Principles
subtopics.definition: Core security principles are the design rules behind controls: protect confidentiality, integrity and availability, layer defenses, grant least privilege and separate duties.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These principles let a practitioner judge whether a control set is sound without knowing every product. Gaps against them, such as one control guarding everything, point to concentrated risk.
how_it_works: Confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) name what an event harms, which shapes the impact rating.
Layered controls of different kinds mean one failure does not expose the asset.
Each user and system gets only the access its role needs, for only as long as needed.
Critical tasks are split so no one person can complete and hide a harmful action.
Where duties cannot be split, compensating controls such as independent review reduce the risk.
subtopics.example: A credit union protects its member database mainly with a strong perimeter firewall; inside, every staff account can read all records. Farah, the IT risk analyst, explains to the chief operating officer that one phished account would expose everything, and proposes layered controls: role-based access, database monitoring and multifactor authentication.

review: Compare access rights with job roles to find excess privilege
Inspect critical processes for one person holding conflicting duties
evidence: Access review results with removals signed by managers
Conflict reports generated by the identity management system
audit_focus.recommend: Have system owners remove excess access and add compensating review where duties cannot be split.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner signs off any access risk left after review

subtopics.isaca_rule: No single control is enough for a critical asset. Look for layered, independent controls, least privilege and separated duties; where a principle cannot be met, the risk is recorded and compensated, and the owner accepts what remains within appetite.

exam_traps.trap: Relying on one strong perimeter control to protect everything inside.
exam_traps.why: Once an attacker or insider is past the perimeter, nothing else stops them. Layers inside the network limit how far one failure spreads.

key_terms.definition: Layering several independent controls so one failure does not expose an asset.
Giving users and systems only the access needed for their tasks.
Splitting conflicting steps, such as initiating, recording and holding assets, among people so no one can complete and conceal misuse alone.
Access to specific information only when a current task needs it, even if role or clearance allows more; least privilege limits actions once there.
Elevated access granted for a specific task and a limited time, then removed, instead of standing administrator rights.

subtopics.name: Zero Trust Architecture
subtopics.definition: Zero Trust is a security approach that grants no implicit trust based on network location; each access request is checked using identity, device state and policy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Remote work, cloud and partners have dissolved the network edge. Zero Trust limits how far a stolen account or infected device can reach, lowering the impact of the most common attack paths.
how_it_works: NIST SP 800-207 sets out tenets, including that all data sources and services count as resources, all communication is secured regardless of location, and access is granted per session.
Decisions use identity, device health, behavior and data sensitivity, and are re-checked over time.
Least privilege and micro-segmentation keep each user or workload to what it needs.
Monitoring of assets and access feeds back into policy decisions.
Adoption is incremental: NIST SP 800-207 describes moving one business process at a time, often piloting on a lower-risk process, to protect the highest-value data.
Until a rollout covers a scenario's users and assets, the register credits only the coverage that is live and working; the finished rollout is target risk.
subtopics.example: A manufacturer's engineers connect to plant systems through a remote access link that, once joined, reaches the whole network. Yusuf, the risk analyst, maps this to a ransomware scenario rated above appetite and proposes a phased Zero Trust plan, starting with per-application access to plant control systems, for the CIO and plant director to prioritize.

review: Trace access to critical applications to per-session identity and device checks
Compare network paths open to remote users with their actual needs
evidence: Access policy configuration showing device and identity conditions
Network flow data showing lateral connections between segments
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CIO approve a phased Zero Trust roadmap that starts with the highest-rated risk scenarios.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management funds and sequences the Zero Trust program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Zero Trust is a strategy that reduces impact by removing implicit trust; it is not one product. The practitioner judges it by the risk it reduces for critical assets and recommends a phased, risk-prioritized path; owners fund and sequence it.

exam_traps.trap: Believing that buying a Zero Trust product makes the organization Zero Trust.
exam_traps.why: Zero Trust is an architecture and set of principles across identity, devices, networks and data. A tool can support it but cannot deliver it alone.

key_terms.definition: Trust granted automatically because of network location or past access, not checked for each request.
Dividing a network into small zones so each workload talks only to what it needs.
The Zero Trust component that decides whether to allow each access request.

subtopics.name: Security Frameworks and Standards
subtopics.definition: Security frameworks and standards are structured sets of outcomes, controls or requirements, such as NIST CSF 2.0 or ISO/IEC 27001, used to organize and benchmark security.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks give a common language for current and target state, help align practice with regulation and contracts, and show gaps. They describe what good looks like, not the organization's actual risk.
how_it_works: NIST CSF 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
Profiles compare the current state with a target state chosen by risk and business needs.
ISO/IEC 27001 sets requirements for an information security management system that can be certified.
A framework is tailored: controls and target Tiers are chosen by risk and cost-benefit, so different units can rightly have different targets.
Certification shows a management system met a standard within a scope on a date; it does not prove risk is low.
A register rating records current risk; it moves when a scenario is reassessed on evidence, not because a profile or certificate changed.
subtopics.example: A software firm wins a contract partly on its ISO/IEC 27001 certificate. Noor, the risk lead, notices the certificate's scope covers only the head office, not the cloud platform that will host the client's data. Noor reports the gap to the chief operating officer and proposes a risk assessment of the platform against the contract's requirements.

review: Compare certificate scope with the systems that hold critical data
Trace gaps in the current profile to planned risk treatments
evidence: Certificate and statement of scope from the certifying body
Current and target profiles with prioritized gaps
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CISO extend assessment to critical systems outside the certified scope and report gaps to risk owners.
audit_focus.decides: Risk owners decide which framework gaps to treat and when

subtopics.isaca_rule: Frameworks organize and benchmark; risk assessment decides. Certification or framework alignment is evidence, not proof of low risk. The practitioner checks scope and fit, then uses the gaps to inform treatment by the owners.

exam_traps.trap: Treating a framework certification as proof that risk is low.
exam_traps.why: Certification covers a scope at a point in time against a standard's requirements. Risk depends on threats, assets and controls outside that snapshot.

key_terms.definition: A description of current or target outcomes for an organization, used to find and prioritize gaps.
The boundaries, such as sites, systems and processes, that a certificate covers.
Adjusting a framework's controls to the organization's risks, systems and obligations.
NIST CSF 2.0 rating of how rigorous risk governance and management practices are: Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable or Adaptive.

topics.overview: This topic covers how people become part of the control system: a risk-aware culture where staff speak up, training matched to each role's risks, and measures that show whether behavior actually changed. It includes fair phishing simulations and awareness of shadow AI, where staff use unapproved AI tools with company data.
can_do: Choose an awareness measure that shows behavior change, not attendance
Run phishing simulations as coaching rather than a trap
Respond to shadow AI with guidance and an approved alternative

subtopics.name: Risk-Aware Culture and Role-Based Training
subtopics.definition: A risk-aware culture is one where people at every level understand the risks in their work, speak up about them and act within appetite, supported by targeted training.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most controls depend on people. Where staff fear blame or see risk as someone else's job, problems stay hidden until they become incidents; where they speak up, risk is found early.
how_it_works: Leaders set the tone by discussing risk openly and rewarding early reporting.
Awareness reaches everyone; role-based training gives deeper skills to people with specific risk duties.
Training content follows the risk profile, such as payment fraud for finance staff or secure coding for developers.
Reporting channels are easy and safe, and reports get visible follow-up.
Mistakes lead to process fixes first; discipline is for willful or repeated misconduct.
subtopics.example: At a pharmaceutical distributor, help desk staff know that password resets skip identity checks at busy times, but they stopped reporting it after past reports led to blame for the shift. Rosa, the risk analyst, raises this with the service desk director as a culture risk and proposes a no-blame reporting channel with visible fixes.

review: Compare training content with the top risks for each role
Analyze incident and near-miss reports for signs of underreporting
evidence: Training records mapped to the risk duties of each role
Culture survey results and reporting-channel volumes
audit_focus.recommend: Have senior management sponsor safe reporting channels and training tied to each role's place in the risk profile.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management owns the risk culture and funds the program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Culture is a control. The practitioner promotes risk awareness, makes sure training matches roles and risks, and treats hidden or blamed errors as a process signal. Leadership owns the culture; the practitioner helps measure and improve it.

exam_traps.trap: Blaming the user who made an error instead of fixing the process that allowed it.
exam_traps.why: Blame discourages reporting, so future problems stay hidden. Most errors point to a design or process weakness that a control can fix.

key_terms.definition: The values and beliefs people across the enterprise share about risk, and the behavior they drive.
Training matched to the specific risk duties of a job, beyond general awareness.
The example leaders set, through words and actions, about how seriously risk is taken.

subtopics.name: Measuring Awareness, Phishing Simulations and Shadow AI
subtopics.definition: Measuring awareness means tracking whether behavior changes after training, using measures such as reporting rates and simulation results, not just course completion.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Completion rates show who clicked through a course, not who acts safely. Behavior measures show whether training reduces risk and where to focus, including new risks such as staff pasting data into public AI tools.
how_it_works: Outcome measures include phishing report rates, repeat-click rates, policy exceptions and incidents caused by error.
Fair simulations are announced as a program, avoid cruel lures, coach rather than shame and report trends, not names.
Results are compared over time and by role to target follow-up training.
Shadow AI, staff using unapproved AI tools, is an awareness topic: what data may go where and which tools are approved.
Awareness works best paired with an approved alternative, because bans without options push use underground.
subtopics.example: A transport authority reports 99% completion of its phishing course, yet monthly simulations show the same teams clicking and few staff reporting. Jordan, the risk analyst, proposes adding report and repeat-click rates to the awareness report and coaching for repeat clickers instead of discipline, and asks the chief operating officer to sponsor the change.

review: Compare awareness metrics with incident trends caused by human error
Inspect simulation rules for fairness, coaching and data handling
evidence: Simulation trend data showing report and repeat-click rates
Data-loss tool alerts on uploads to unapproved AI services
audit_focus.recommend: Have the awareness program owner report behavior measures alongside completion and target follow-up by role.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets awareness priorities and approves AI tool choices

subtopics.isaca_rule: Measure behavior, not attendance. The best awareness metric shows changed behavior linked to a risk, such as reporting rates. Simulations teach rather than trap. For shadow AI, pair clear guidance with an approved tool.

exam_traps.trap: Using training completion rates as the main measure of awareness.
exam_traps.why: Completion proves exposure to content, not changed behavior. A fully trained workforce can still click links or leak data.

exam_traps.trap: Naming and disciplining staff who fail a phishing simulation.
exam_traps.why: Shaming lowers trust and reporting. Simulations work best as coaching, with trends reported and repeat cases handled through extra training.

key_terms.definition: A safe, fake phishing message sent to staff so they can practice spotting and reporting real ones.
Use of AI tools for work without the organization's approval or controls.
The share of staff who report a suspicious message, a leading sign of awareness.

topics.topic_name: Data Privacy and Data Protection Principles
topics.overview: This topic covers how personal data is handled fairly and lawfully: purpose limitation, minimization, lawful basis and individual rights; privacy by design and privacy impact assessments; and the added risks when personal data feeds AI or crosses borders. The core lesson is that privacy and security overlap but are not the same.
can_do: Tell a privacy failure from a security failure in a scenario
Place a privacy impact assessment at the right point in a project
Check purpose, basis, location and vendor data use before personal data reaches an AI service

subtopics.name: Privacy Principles
subtopics.definition: Privacy principles are rules for fair handling of personal data, including purpose limitation, data minimization, a lawful basis such as consent, transparency and individual rights.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Privacy harm affects people and brings regulatory, legal and trust consequences. A secure system can still breach privacy if it collects too much or uses data for an undisclosed purpose.
how_it_works: The purpose is decided and stated before collection, and data is not used later in ways incompatible with it.
Only the data the purpose needs is collected and kept.
People are told what happens to their data, and the organization has a valid basis, such as consent.
People can access, correct or delete their data, depending on the law that applies.
Security protects data from unauthorized access; privacy also governs authorized use.

rows.label: Main question
cells: Is the data protected from unauthorized access?
Is the data handled fairly and lawfully, even by authorized users?

subtopics.example: A fitness app's product team proposes selling users' location history to advertisers, arguing the data is already encrypted and well protected. Kenji, the privacy risk analyst, explains that encryption does not change the purpose users agreed to, and asks the product owner and privacy officer to assess the proposal against the stated purpose and consent.

review: Compare data collected with the purposes in the privacy notice
Trace new uses of personal data to a documented purpose review
evidence: Privacy notices and consent records with dates and versions
Records of processing listing purposes and data categories
audit_focus.recommend: Have the privacy officer review every new use of personal data against its stated purpose before launch.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides on use, with the privacy officer's advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Privacy is not the same as security. Ask whether the purpose was set before collection and whether the use matches it; strong encryption does not make an unfair use acceptable. The data owner and privacy officer decide, with legal advice.

exam_traps.trap: Assuming encrypted data has no privacy risk.
exam_traps.why: Encryption stops outsiders reading data. It does nothing about an organization using the data beyond what people agreed to.

exam_traps.trap: Collecting data first and deciding how to use it later.
exam_traps.why: Purpose limitation requires the purpose to be set and stated before collection. Data gathered without one is excess risk.

key_terms.definition: Personal data is gathered only for clearly stated, lawful purposes, and later use must fit them; an unrelated new use needs its own legal basis.
Collecting and keeping only the personal data the purpose needs.
Any information that tells you about a particular person, or lets someone work out who they are, alone or combined with other data.

subtopics.name: Privacy by Design and Privacy Impact Assessment
subtopics.definition: Privacy by design builds privacy protections into systems from the start, and a privacy impact assessment (PIA) analyzes how a system handles personal data and the risks involved.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Privacy fixes after launch are costly and may come after people are harmed. A PIA at the design stage finds problems while they are cheap to fix and gives owners a documented basis for decisions.
