how_it_works: A PIA is run before building or buying technology that processes personal data, or starting a new collection.
It maps data flows, assesses risks to individuals and the organization, and proposes mitigations.
Privacy by design sets protective defaults, such as minimal collection and short retention.
The PIA is updated when the system, purpose or data changes.
The NIST Privacy Framework helps organize privacy risk work alongside cybersecurity risk.
subtopics.example: A public library plans self-checkout kiosks with face recognition to speed lending. Tomas, the risk analyst, recommends a privacy impact assessment before the vendor is chosen. The assessment shows a card-and-PIN option meets the goal without biometric data, and Tomas presents both options with their risks to the library director.

review: Trace new systems handling personal data to a PIA before build
Compare PIA mitigations with the controls actually implemented
evidence: Completed PIAs with dates, data flows and mitigations
Project gate records showing PIA approval
audit_focus.recommend: Have project sponsors complete a PIA at design and update it whenever purpose or data changes.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts residual privacy risk with the privacy officer's advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assess privacy before the design is fixed. The best time for a PIA is early, before build or purchase, and its results go to the owner as options. Privacy by design favors the option that meets the goal with less personal data.

exam_traps.trap: Running the privacy impact assessment after the system is built, to document what was done.
exam_traps.why: A late PIA can only describe risks, not design them out. Its value comes from shaping requirements before commitments are made.

key_terms.definition: A diagram of how personal data moves between people, systems and third parties.
Settings that give the most privacy protection without the user having to act.
In the NIST Privacy Framework, a data operation that could cause problems for individuals.

subtopics.name: Personal Data in AI and Cross-Border Transfers
subtopics.definition: Personal data in AI and cross-border transfers create risk when personal data trains or feeds AI systems, or moves to a country with different legal protections.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI can infer sensitive facts, memorize training data and make decisions about people, and data sent abroad may fall under weaker or conflicting laws. Both raise legal exposure and harm to individuals.
how_it_works: Check the lawful basis and purpose before using personal data to train or prompt an AI system.
Minimize or de-identify data where the purpose allows, knowing de-identified data can sometimes be re-identified.
Assess AI outputs for privacy harm, such as inferences about health or exposure of training data.
Before transferring data abroad, confirm the legal mechanism and the protections at the destination.
Contracts with AI and cloud providers set where data is stored, whether it trains their models and how it is deleted.
Removing names is not enough when exact times, places or rare details remain, because those records can be linked back to the people involved.
subtopics.example: A hospital group wants to send patient notes to an overseas AI transcription service. Chidi, the privacy risk analyst, checks where the data will be processed, whether the vendor trains its models on customer data and what transfer rules apply. Chidi asks legal counsel to confirm the transfer basis and reports the findings to the clinical director.

review: Trace personal data sent to AI services to a purpose and lawful basis
Compare vendor data-use terms with the organization's privacy commitments
evidence: Transfer assessments naming destination countries and safeguards
AI vendor contracts covering training use, location and deletion
audit_focus.recommend: Have the privacy officer and legal counsel approve any transfer of personal data to AI or overseas services.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides, with legal counsel and the privacy officer advising

subtopics.isaca_rule: Personal data keeps its privacy rules inside AI and across borders. The practitioner checks purpose, lawful basis, minimization, location and vendor data use before the data moves; legal counsel advises on the law and the data owner decides.

exam_traps.trap: Assuming a vendor's AI service may use customer data however its standard terms allow.
exam_traps.why: The organization remains accountable for personal data it shares. Terms on training use, location and deletion must fit its own obligations.

key_terms.definition: Removing or altering identifiers so data no longer readily points to a person.
Linking de-identified data back to a person using other information.
Moving personal data, or allowing access to it, from one country to another.

key_terminologies.Enterprise architecture (EA): The documented model of how business processes, data, applications and technology fit together to deliver strategy.
key_terminologies.Technology roadmap: A time-based plan of which technologies will be adopted, upgraded or retired, linked to business goals.
key_terminologies.Technical debt: The future cost and risk created by shortcuts, deferred upgrades or aging technology.
key_terminologies.Change management: The controlled process for assessing, approving, testing, implementing and reviewing changes.
key_terminologies.Emergency change: A change made fast to restore service or stop harm, then documented and reviewed after the fact.
key_terminologies.Incident management: The process for logging, prioritizing and resolving incidents so the affected service is back in use quickly.
key_terminologies.Problem management: The process that finds and removes the root cause of one or more incidents.
key_terminologies.CI/CD pipeline: The automated path that builds, tests and deploys code changes to production.
key_terminologies.System development life cycle (SDLC): The phases of a system from initiation through design, build, test, operation and disposal.
key_terminologies.Secure Software Development Framework (S: NIST SP 800-218, a set of practices for building security into any software development model.
key_terminologies.Data owner: The business manager accountable for a set of data: its quality (integrity and accuracy), proper use and protection. They classify it and decide who may access it and how long it is kept.
key_terminologies.Data custodian: The party, often IT, that stores and protects data according to the owner's rules.
key_terminologies.Sanitization: Making data on storage media unrecoverable, by clearing, purging or destroying it.
key_terminologies.Portfolio management: Selecting and prioritizing programs and projects by value, risk and strategic fit.
key_terminologies.Definition of done: The agreed criteria, including control criteria, an Agile work item must meet to be complete.
key_terminologies.Recovery time objective (RTO): The target for how soon a business function, or a resource it depends on, must be working again after a disruption, set by the business within the maximum tolerable outage.
key_terminologies.Recovery point objective (RPO): How far back in time recovered data may be after a disruption, set from how much data loss the business can accept; it drives how often data is backed up or replicated.
key_terminologies.Maximum tolerable outage (MTO): ISACA's term for the outage limit of a critical process or system: past it, the damage to the enterprise becomes significant, so recovery must be complete within it. Other sources say maximum tolerable downtime (MTD).
key_terminologies.Hot site: An alternate site equipped and configured to take over processing within minutes to hours.
key_terminologies.Immutable backup: A backup copy that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, even by administrators.
key_terminologies.Emerging technology: A technology new to the organization or the market whose risks and benefits are not yet well understood.
key_terminologies.Model drift: Loss of an AI model's accuracy over time as real-world data moves away from the training data.
key_terminologies.Defense in depth: Layering several independent controls so one failure does not expose an asset.
key_terminologies.Zero Trust: A security approach that grants no implicit trust based on network location and checks every access request.
key_terminologies.NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0: A NIST framework of cybersecurity outcomes in six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
key_terminologies.Risk-aware culture: A culture where people understand the risks in their work, speak up and act within appetite.
key_terminologies.Shadow AI: Use of AI tools for work without the organization's approval or controls.
key_terminologies.Purpose limitation: A privacy principle: personal data is gathered only for clearly stated, lawful purposes, and any later use must fit those purposes; an unrelated new use needs its own legal basis.
key_terminologies.Privacy impact assessment (PIA): An analysis of how a system or activity handles personal data, its privacy risks and mitigations.
